# binwidth of 0.5 (small bins)

  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +

text: In this section we will practice calculating probabilities using different probability distributions. In the last section, we worked with the binomial distribution; now, we turn to the normal distribution.

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
text:
Normal Distributions
Unlike the binomial distribution, which describes a discrete outcome (a count), the normal distribution describes a continuous outcome. It is a bell-shaped, symmetric distribution defined by two parameters: the mean (\(\mu\)) and the standard deviation (\(\sigma\)).
We will use the following running example: birth weight in the U.S. can be reasonably modeled with a normal distribution with a mean of 3,250 grams and a standard deviation of 550 grams. A birth weight of 2,500 grams or less is considered “low birth weight.”

Visualizing the Normal Distribution
To start, let’s get a sense of what this distribution looks like by simulating a large number of birth weights and plotting the results.

Fill in the code below to randomly draw 100,000 birth weights from a normal distribution with mean = 3250 and sd = 550. Save the result in a data frame called births with a column called weight. Then plot a histogram of the simulated weights.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)
# simulate birth weights from a normal distribution
births = data.frame(weight = rnorm(n = , mean = , sd = ))

# plot the distribution
births %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weight)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)
# simulate birth weights from a normal distribution
births = data.frame(weight = rnorm(n = 100000, mean = 3250, sd = 550))

# plot the distribution
births %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weight)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()
You should see a bell-shaped, symmetric histogram centered around 3,250, with most values falling roughly between 1,600 and 4,900 (within 3 standard deviations of the mean). Since this is randomly generated, the exact shape of your bars may differ slightly depending on your R version and setup, but the overall shape and center should look the same.




Check the mean and standard deviation of your simulated births$weight column using mean() and sd(). Are they close to the true parameters (3250 and 550) we used to generate the data? Why aren’t they exactly equal?


Just like with the binomial distribution, we could use this simulated data to estimate probabilities empirically. However, because the normal distribution has a known mathematical form, R gives us functions to calculate exact probabilities directly—no simulation required.


Normal Probabilities in R
Recall the key functions for working with the normal distribution:

pnorm(q, mean, sd) gives \(P(X \le q)\) from a \(X \sim Normal(mean, sd)\) distribution
pnorm(q, mean, sd, lower.tail = FALSE) gives \(P(X > q)\)
qnorm(p, mean, sd) gives the value \(x\) such that \(P(X \le x) = p\) (i.e., the inverse of pnorm)

If you don’t specify mean and sd, R assumes you want the standard normal distribution (\(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma = 1\)).


Calculating a Lower-Tail Probability

Use pnorm() to find the probability that a randomly selected newborn has low birth weight (birth weight \(\le\) 2,500 grams), assuming birth weight follows a \(Normal(3250, 550)\) distribution.

# probability of low birth weight
pnorm(q = , mean = , sd = )






Solution





# probability of low birth weight
pnorm(q = 2500, mean = 3250, sd = 550)
[1] 0.08634102
There is about an 8.6% chance that a randomly selected newborn has low birth weight.





Standardizing: Working with Z-Scores
Instead of working directly with birth weight (\(X\)), we can standardize to the standard normal distribution by converting to a Z-score: \(Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\). A Z-score tells us how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.

First, calculate the Z-score corresponding to a birth weight of 2,500 grams (using \(\mu = 3250\) and \(\sigma = 550\)). Then use pnorm() on that Z-score (using the default mean and sd, i.e. the standard normal) to confirm you get the same probability as above.

# calculate the Z-score for a birth weight of 2500 grams
z = ( - ) / 

# probability using the standard normal distribution
pnorm(z)






Solution





# calculate the Z-score for a birth weight of 2500 grams
z = (2500 - 3250) / 550
z
[1] -1.363636
# probability using the standard normal distribution
pnorm(z)
[1] 0.08634102
Same answer as before! A birth weight of 2,500 grams is about 1.36 standard deviations below the mean.





Calculating an Upper-Tail Probability

Suppose birth weights above 4,000 grams are flagged as unusually high. Use pnorm() with lower.tail = FALSE to find the probability that a randomly selected newborn’s weight exceeds 4,000 grams.

# probability of birth weight greater than 4000 grams
pnorm(q = , mean = , sd = , lower.tail = )






Solution





# probability of birth weight greater than 4000 grams
pnorm(q = 4000, mean = 3250, sd = 550, lower.tail = F)
[1] 0.08634102
Notice this is the same probability we calculated for low birth weight! That’s not a coincidence: 2,500 is 750 grams below the mean (3250), and 4,000 is 750 grams above the mean. Because the normal distribution is symmetric, \(P(X \le \mu - c) = P(X \ge \mu + c)\) for any constant \(c\).





Calculating a Middle Probability

Find the probability that a randomly selected birth weight falls between 2,700 and 3,800 grams.


# probability of birth weight between 2700 and 3800 grams
pnorm(q = , mean = 3250, sd = 550) - pnorm(q = , mean = 3250, sd = 550)






Solution





# probability of birth weight between 2700 and 3800 grams
pnorm(q = 3800, mean = 3250, sd = 550) - pnorm(q = 2700, mean = 3250, sd = 550)
[1] 0.6826895
Notice that 2,700 and 3,800 are exactly one standard deviation below and above the mean (3250 − 550 = 2700; 3250 + 550 = 3800). This is why the probability is so close to 68%—this is the Empirical Rule in action!




Using what you know about the Empirical Rule, what would you expect the probability to be that a birth weight falls between 2,150 and 4,350 grams (within 2 standard deviations of the mean)? Check your intuition using pnorm().




Working Backwards with qnorm()
Sometimes we want to go the other direction: instead of starting with a value and finding a probability, we start with a probability and find the corresponding value. This is what qnorm() does.

Find the birth weight that corresponds to the 10th percentile of the distribution (i.e., the value below which only 10% of birth weights fall).

# birth weight at the 10th percentile
qnorm(p = , mean = , sd = )






Solution





# birth weight at the 10th percentile
qnorm(p = 0.1, mean = 3250, sd = 550)
[1] 2545.147
Only 10% of newborns in this population have a birth weight below about 2,545 grams.




Now find the range of birth weights that captures the middle 95% of the distribution (i.e., the values corresponding to the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles). Hint: you can pass a vector of probabilities, c(0.025, 0.975), to qnorm() to get both values at once.

# birth weight range for the middle 95%
qnorm(p = c(, ), mean = , sd = )






Solution





# birth weight range for the middle 95%
qnorm(p = c(0.025, 0.975), mean = 3250, sd = 550)
[1] 2172.02 4327.98
95% of birth weights in this population fall between about 2,172 grams and 4,328 grams.




In your own words, explain the difference between what pnorm() and qnorm() each calculate. When would you use one versus the other?

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
text:
Recall that if we have a population with some true underlying parameter (like a mean, \(\mu\)), we use a sample statistic (like a sample mean, \(\bar{x}\)) to estimate it. Because our sample is just one of many possible samples we could have drawn, our statistic will vary from sample to sample. The sampling distribution of a statistic describes what values that statistic would take on across all possible samples of a given size, \(n\), drawn from the same population.
In this section, we’ll start from a simulated population, then repeatedly sample from it to see visualize the sampling distribution of the mean.
Our running example: length of hospital stay (LOS), in days, following a particular surgery. LOS tends to be right-skewed—most patients go home quickly, but a few stay much longer—so it’s a nice example for testing whether the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) really works even when the underlying population isn’t normal.


To explore sampling distributions, we first need a population to sample from. We’ve simulated one for you below: 100,000 patients’ length of stay, drawn from an exponential distribution with a mean of 4.5 days. The results are saved in a data frame called pop, with a column called los. (You don’t need to worry about the code that generated it—just know that we now have a full population to sample from.)

Fill in the code below to plot a histogram of the population distribution, pop$los, to see its shape.

# plot the population distribution
pop %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = )) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





# plot the population distribution
pop %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = los)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()
You should see a strongly right-skewed distribution: a tall bar near 0, with a long tail stretching out to the right toward higher values. This is clearly not a normal distribution.



We can check the population’s mean and standard deviation directly:
# mean and sd of the population
mean(pop$los)
sd(pop$los)

What is the mean value of los in the population? What is the standard deviaiton?





In practice, we don’t get to see the whole population—we only get to observe one sample. Let’s draw a single sample of patients and calculate the sample mean.

Draw one random sample of 30 patients (without replacement) from the population vector pop$los, and calculate the mean of that sample.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1)
# draw one sample of size 30
one_sample = sample(pop$los, size = , replace = FALSE)

# calculate the sample mean
mean(one_sample)






Solution





# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1)
# draw one sample of size 30
one_sample = sample(pop$los, size = 30, replace = FALSE)

# calculate the sample mean
mean(one_sample)
Your sample mean is a single point estimate of the true population mean (4.5). If you re-ran this code with a different seed, you’d get a different sample, and therefore a different sample mean. That sample-to-sample variability is exactly what the sampling distribution describes.






To see the sampling distribution of the mean directly, we need to repeat the sampling process many times—drawing a sample, calculating its mean, and recording that mean—over and over. Let’s do this for samples of size n = 5 first.

Fill in the code below to repeat the sampling process 10,000 times, each time drawing a sample of size 5 from the population and recording the sample mean.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(2)
# number of repeated samples to draw
niter = 10000

# create a place to store the sample means
samp_means_5 = data.frame(mean_los = rep(NA, 10000))

for(i in 1:niter){
  # draw one sample of size 5
  samp = sample(pop$los, size = , replace = FALSE)
  # store the sample mean
  samp_means_5$mean_los[i] = mean(samp)
}

# plot the sampling distribution
samp_means_5 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_los)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "orange", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





The plotted distribution should still look somewhat right-skewed, though a bit less extreme than the population itself. With such a small sample size (n = 5), each sample mean is still heavily influenced by any large values that happen to get sampled.



Now let’s repeat the same process, but with a much larger sample size, n = 100.

Repeat the process above, but this time draw samples of size 100 instead of size 5.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(2)
# number of repeated samples to draw
niter = 10000

# create a place to store the sample means
samp_means_100 = data.frame(mean_los = rep(NA, niter))

for(i in 1:niter){
  # draw one sample of size 100
  samp = sample(pop$los, size = , replace = FALSE)
  # store the sample mean
  samp_means_100$mean_los[i] = mean(samp)
}

# plot the sampling distribution
samp_means_100 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_los)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "orange", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





Even though the population is strongly right-skewed, the sampling distribution of the mean for n = 100 should look approximately symmetric and bell-shaped—much closer to a normal distribution. This is the Central Limit Theorem in action: as the sample size grows, the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the shape of the underlying population (as long as \(n\) is reasonably large).




Compare the spread (width) of the two sampling distributions you just created (n = 5 vs. n = 100). Which one is more spread out? Does this match what you’d expect based on the sample sizes used?





The standard deviation of a sampling distribution has a special name: the standard error (SE). The CLT tells us that if \(X\) has population mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), then for a sufficiently large sample size \(n\):
\[\bar{X} \sim Normal\left(\mu, \ \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
That is, the theoretical standard error is \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\).

Calculate the empirical standard error from your simulated sampling distribution for n = 100 (i.e., sd() of samp_means_100$mean_los). Then calculate the theoretical standard error using the formula above, assuming the true population standard deviation is 4.5 (recall: for the exponential distribution, sd = mean) and n = 100.

# empirical standard error (from our simulation)
sd(samp_means_100$mean_los)

# theoretical standard error
 / sqrt()






Solution





# theoretical standard error
4.5 / sqrt(100)
[1] 0.45
Your empirical standard error (from sd(samp_means_100$mean_los)) should be close to 0.45, though it won’t match exactly since it’s based on a finite number of simulated samples. Notice that as \(n\) increases, the standard error decreases—larger samples give us more precise (less variable) estimates of the population mean.

Solution





# plot the population distribution
pop %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = los)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()
You should see a strongly right-skewed distribution: a tall bar near 0, with a long tail stretching out to the right toward higher values. This is clearly not a normal distribution.



We can check the population’s mean and standard deviation directly:
# mean and sd of the population
mean(pop$los)
sd(pop$los)

What is the mean value of los in the population? What is the standard deviaiton?





In practice, we don’t get to see the whole population—we only get to observe one sample. Let’s draw a single sample of patients and calculate the sample mean.

Draw one random sample of 30 patients (without replacement) from the population vector pop$los, and calculate the mean of that sample.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1)
# draw one sample of size 30
one_sample = sample(pop$los, size = , replace = FALSE)

# calculate the sample mean
mean(one_sample)






Solution





# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1)
# draw one sample of size 30
one_sample = sample(pop$los, size = 30, replace = FALSE)

# calculate the sample mean
mean(one_sample)
Your sample mean is a single point estimate of the true population mean (4.5). If you re-ran this code with a different seed, you’d get a different sample, and therefore a different sample mean. That sample-to-sample variability is exactly what the sampling distribution describes.






To see the sampling distribution of the mean directly, we need to repeat the sampling process many times—drawing a sample, calculating its mean, and recording that mean—over and over. Let’s do this for samples of size n = 5 first.

Fill in the code below to repeat the sampling process 10,000 times, each time drawing a sample of size 5 from the population and recording the sample mean.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(2)
# number of repeated samples to draw
niter = 10000

# create a place to store the sample means
samp_means_5 = data.frame(mean_los = rep(NA, 10000))

for(i in 1:niter){
  # draw one sample of size 5
  samp = sample(pop$los, size = , replace = FALSE)
  # store the sample mean
  samp_means_5$mean_los[i] = mean(samp)
}

# plot the sampling distribution
samp_means_5 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_los)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "orange", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





The plotted distribution should still look somewhat right-skewed, though a bit less extreme than the population itself. With such a small sample size (n = 5), each sample mean is still heavily influenced by any large values that happen to get sampled.



Now let’s repeat the same process, but with a much larger sample size, n = 100.

Repeat the process above, but this time draw samples of size 100 instead of size 5.

# set random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(2)
# number of repeated samples to draw
niter = 10000

# create a place to store the sample means
samp_means_100 = data.frame(mean_los = rep(NA, niter))

for(i in 1:niter){
  # draw one sample of size 100
  samp = sample(pop$los, size = , replace = FALSE)
  # store the sample mean
  samp_means_100$mean_los[i] = mean(samp)
}

# plot the sampling distribution
samp_means_100 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_los)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "orange", bins = 40) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





Even though the population is strongly right-skewed, the sampling distribution of the mean for n = 100 should look approximately symmetric and bell-shaped—much closer to a normal distribution. This is the Central Limit Theorem in action: as the sample size grows, the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the shape of the underlying population (as long as \(n\) is reasonably large).




Compare the spread (width) of the two sampling distributions you just created (n = 5 vs. n = 100). Which one is more spread out? Does this match what you’d expect based on the sample sizes used?





The standard deviation of a sampling distribution has a special name: the standard error (SE). The CLT tells us that if \(X\) has population mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), then for a sufficiently large sample size \(n\):
\[\bar{X} \sim Normal\left(\mu, \ \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
That is, the theoretical standard error is \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\).

Calculate the empirical standard error from your simulated sampling distribution for n = 100 (i.e., sd() of samp_means_100$mean_los). Then calculate the theoretical standard error using the formula above, assuming the true population standard deviation is 4.5 (recall: for the exponential distribution, sd = mean) and n = 100.

# empirical standard error (from our simulation)
sd(samp_means_100$mean_los)

# theoretical standard error
 / sqrt()






Solution





# theoretical standard error
4.5 / sqrt(100)
[1] 0.45
Your empirical standard error (from sd(samp_means_100$mean_los)) should be close to 0.45, though it won’t match exactly since it’s based on a finite number of simulated samples. Notice that as \(n\) increases, the standard error decreases—larger samples give us more precise (less variable) estimates of the population mean.

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
section: Applying the CLT to Calculate Probabilities
text:
Applying the CLT to Calculate Probabilities
Once we know (or can assume) that a sampling distribution is approximately normal, we can use everything we learned about the normal distribution to calculate probabilities about sample means—without needing to simulate anything!

Suppose we plan to take a random sample of 100 patients. Assuming the population mean LOS is 4.5 days with a standard deviation of 4.5 days, use the CLT to find the probability that the sample mean LOS is greater than 5 days. Hint: first calculate the standard error, then use pnorm().

# standard error for n = 100
se = 4.5 / sqrt()

# probability the sample mean exceeds 5 days
pnorm(q = , mean = , sd = se, lower.tail = )






Solution





# standard error for n = 100
se = 4.5 / sqrt(100)

# probability the sample mean exceeds 5 days
pnorm(q = 5, mean = 4.5, sd = se, lower.tail = F)
[1] 0.1332603
There is about a 13.3% chance that a random sample of 100 patients has a mean LOS greater than 5 days.




Now repeat the same calculation, but assume we only sampled 30 patients instead of 100. Is the probability higher, lower, or the same compared to before?

# standard error for n = 30
se = 4.5 / sqrt()

# probability the sample mean exceeds 5 days
pnorm(q = , mean = , sd = se, lower.tail = )






Solution





# standard error for n = 30
se = 4.5 / sqrt(30)

# probability the sample mean exceeds 5 days
pnorm(q = 5, mean = 4.5, sd = se, lower.tail = F)
[1] 0.2714012
With a smaller sample size (n = 30), the standard error is larger, so sample means are more variable. This makes it more likely (about 27.1% vs. 13.3%) to see a sample mean as far from 4.5 as 5 days, just by chance.




We used the CLT to calculate these probabilities even though our population (length of stay) is not normally distributed. Based on what you saw in the “Building a Sampling Distribution” section, explain why this is still valid for n = 100 but might be questionable for a much smaller sample size, like n = 5. What if I wanted to calculate the probability that one individual length of stay was above some value? Could I use the CLT then?


Notice that if the underlying population itself were normally distributed, we would not need a large sample size for the CLT to apply—the sampling distribution of the mean would be exactly normal for any sample size, even n = 2 or n = 3. The “large enough n” condition is only needed to overcome skewness or other non-normal features of the population.

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
text:
Binomial Distribution
We will begin with the binomial distribution.
We are interested in studying hand hygiene practices at a local hospital. Suppose that the probability of a healthcare worker following proper hand hygiene practices is 75%. We plan to observe 15 healthcare workers and will record if they comply with health hygiene recommendations or not.
We are going to start by empirically drawing from a binomial distribution to get a sense of what it looks like. Then we will use R functions to calculate probabilities directly from a binomial distribution.

Fill in the code below to randomly draw one sample (n = 1) from a binomial distribution with 15 healthcare workers and a p = 0.75 probability of compliance with hand hygiene recommendations.

# sample one time from a binomial distribution (note, n = 1 indicates we are observing one set of 15 healthcare workers)
rbinom(n = 1, size = , p = )







Solution





# sample one time from a binomial distribution (note, n = 1 indicates we are observing one set of 15 healthcare workers)
rbinom(n = 1, size = 15, p = 0.75)



If you completed the blanks above correctly, should see a number between 0 and 15. This number corresponds to the number out of 15 healthcare workers followed hand hygiene recommendations.






Note



Since this is a random process, we will all see different numbers.
In fact, try clicking the “Run Code” button above a few times. You should see different numbers appear when you run the code multiple times. This is what the code is supposed to do, since it is randomly generating values from this distribution.
For instructional purposes, it will be easier if we all get the same answers. We will show a strategy to address this next.

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
text:
Setting Random Seeds
To help us all get the same answers, we can add a line of code to do something called “setting the random seed.” This is a bit technical, but what you should know is that if we all set the seed to the same number, we should get the same answers so our work will be more reproducible (don’t worry, the results are still random–they’re just a bit easier to keep track of!).
# set random seed for reproducibility (I'm setting it to 123, but the number doesn't matter!)
set.seed(123)
# sample one time from a binomial distribution (note, n = 1 indicates we are observing one set of 15 healthcare workers)
rbinom(n = 1, size = 15, p = 0.75)

Now we should all get the number 12.

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
text:
Drawing Multiple Samples
So far, we have only drawn from this binomial distribution a few times. To get a sense of the shape of the distribution, we will need to sample from it many times. To do this, we will change the argument n in the code above.

Fill in the code below to draw from a binomial distribution multiple times. Start by drawing 5 samples from the distribution, then 10, then 30. Hit “Run Code” each time to see how changing the argument n impacts the output.

# set random seed for reproducibility (I'm setting it to 123, but the number doesn't matter!)
set.seed(123)
# sample from a binomial distribution 
rbinom(n = , size = 15, p = 0.75)







Solution





# set random seed for reproducibility (I'm setting it to 123, but the number doesn't matter!)
set.seed(123)
# sample from a binomial distribution (5 times)
rbinom(n = 5, size = 15, p = 0.75)
[1] 12 10 12 9 9
# sample from a binomial distribution (10 times)
rbinom(n = 10, size = 15, p = 0.75)
[1] 12 10 12 9 9 14 11 9 11 12
# sample from a binomial distribution (30 times)
rbinom(n = 30, size = 15, p = 0.75)
[1] 12 10 12 9 9 14 11 9 11 12 8 12 11 11 13 9 12 14 12 8 9 10 11 7 11 [26] 10 11 11 12 13

text:
Visualizing a Binomial Distribution
Now, let’s draw from the distribution 10,000 times (imagine observing 10,000 different sets of 15 healthcare workers), save the results in a hand hygiene data frame called hh , and visualize the distribution.

Fill in the code below to draw 10,000 samples from the same binomial distribution. The outcomes of these 10,000 draws will be saved in a data frame called hh, which can then be used to plot the distribution.

# set random seed for reproducibility (I'm setting it to 123, but the number doesn't matter!)
set.seed(123)
# sample from a binomial distribution 10,000 times
hh = data.frame(compliant = rbinom(n = , size = , p = ))

# plot the distribution
hh %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = )) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "blue") + 
  theme_bw()
We can also make a table of the number of times each outcome was observed
# table of outcome frequencies
xtabs(~ compliant, data = hh)

Describe the distribution. Which values are the most common? What is the highest value observed? What is the lowest value observed?

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
section: Empirical Probabilities from a Binomial Distribution
text:
Empirical Probabilities from a Binomial Distribution
Now let’s calculate some (empirical) probabilities using our simulated distribution. These won’t be the true theoretical probabilities, but they should be close!


How often do we see all 15 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability all 15
sum(hh$compliant == ) / 10000






Solution





# probability all 15
sum(hh$compliant == 15) / 10000
[1] 0.013





How often do fewer than 10 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability fewer than 10
sum(hh$compliant < ) / 10000







Solution





# probability fewer than 10
sum(hh$compliant < 10) / 10000
[1] 0.1436





How often do at least 12 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability at least 12
sum(hh$compliant ) / 10000






Solution





# probability at least 12
sum(hh$compliant >= 12) / 10000

# alternatively:
# probability at least 12
sum(hh$compliant > 11) / 10000
[1] 0.4641





How often do exactly 2 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability exactly 2
sum(hh$compliant ) / 10000






Solution





# probability exactly 2
sum(hh$compliant == 2) / 10000
sum(hh$compliant > 11) / 10000
[1] 0
Across 10,000 tries, we never observe only 2 out of 15!

title: Module 2: Probability and Inference
text:
Theoretical Probabilities
We saw that only 1.3% of the simulated distribution has a value of 15, 14.36% had a value under 10, and 46.41% had a value of at least 12. Let’s see what these probabilities should be based on the true, theoretical binomial distribution.


What is the true probability that all 15 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability all 15
dbinom(x = , size = 15, prob = 0.75)






Solution





# probability all 15
dbinom(x = 15, size = 15, prob = 0.75)
[1] 0.01336346





What is the true probability that fewer than 10 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability fewer than 10
pbinom(q = , size = 15, prob = 0.75)






Solution





# probability fewer than 10
pbinom(q = 9, size = 15, prob = 0.75)
[1] 0.1483681
Recall that pbinom(q) gives P(X≤q), so if we want strictly less than 10 this is the same as less than or equal to 9





What is the true probability that at least 12 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability at least 12
pbinom(q = , size = 15, prob = 0.75, lower.tail = )






Solution





# probability at least 12
pbinom(q = 11, size = 15, prob = 0.75, lower.tail = F)

# alternatively:
1 - pbinom(q = 11, size = 15, prob = 0.75)
[1] 0.4612869
lower.tail = F means that we are calculating the upper tail; that is, P(X>q) or 1-P(X≤q). Again, since we want to include 12, at least 12 means strictly larger than 11.





What is the true probability that exactly 2 healthcare workers follow hand hygiene recommendations?


# probability exactly 2
dbinom(x = , size = 15, prob = 0.75)






Solution





# probability exactly 2
dbinom(x = 2, size = 15, prob = 0.75)
[1] 8.800998e-07
It is very unlikely to observe 2 out of 15 for this binomial distribution since p=0.75 is quite high.



Notice that the probabilities we have calculated from the theoretical binomial distribution are very similar to the empirical probabilities we calculated from our simulated distribution. This is by design!
We simulated a large sample from a specific distribution to help us visualize what the distribution looks like; that is, to help us understand the relative frequencies of different outcome values from this particular distribution.

title: Module 3: Inference for Numerical Outcomes, Part I
text:
A one-sample t-test is used to make inference about a population mean using a single sample.
Conditions:

Random sample from the population
\(n > 30\), or the original variable follows a normal distribution in the population

\[H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad H_A: \mu \ne \mu_0 \ \ (\text{or} \ <, \ >)\]
where \(\mu\) is the population mean.
Motivating example: A clinical trial is testing a new antihypertensive drug (“Drug A”) against a placebo in patients with Stage 1 hypertension. Each of the 200 patients (100 per group) has a baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP, in mmHg) and a 12-week follow-up SBP. We’ll use this same trial throughout Module 3 to practice different tests. The data are stored in htn_trial, with columns group, sbp_baseline, sbp_followup, and sbp_change (follow-up minus baseline).
For this first test, we’ll focus on a simple question: is the average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group below the clinical hypertension threshold of 130 mmHg?


Right now, the treatment group is stored in htn_trial$group_num as a number (1 = Drug A, 2 = Placebo). If we tried to use this numeric column directly in later analyses (like ANOVA, in Module 4), R would incorrectly treat it as a continuous predictor instead of a grouping variable! Let’s fix that now by creating a proper factor column called group.

Fill in the code below to create a new column, group, that labels group_num == 1 as "Drug A" and group_num == 2 as "Placebo".

# create a labeled factor variable for treatment group
htn_trial = htn_trial %>%
  mutate(group = factor(, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c(, )))

# check that it worked
head(htn_trial)






Solution





# create a labeled factor variable for treatment group
htn_trial = htn_trial %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group_num, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Drug A", "Placebo")))

# check that it worked
head(htn_trial)
You should now see a new column, group, with labels "Drug A" and "Placebo" instead of 1 and 2. We’ll use this labeled version throughout the rest of this document (and throughout Module 3).







Filter htn_trial to only the Drug A group (recall group_num == 1 is Drug A), and plot a histogram of sbp_followup to check the shape of the distribution.

# filter to the Drug A group and plot a histogram of follow-up SBP
htn_trial %>%
  filter( == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = )) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 20) +
  theme_bw()






Solution





# filter to the Drug A group and plot a histogram of follow-up SBP
htn_trial %>%
  filter(group_num == 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sbp_followup)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", bins = 20) +
  theme_bw()
You should see a roughly bell-shaped, symmetric distribution centered somewhere in the 120s. Either way, with n = 100, we’d be comfortable relying on the CLT even if the data were somewhat non-normal.






Suppose a summary of the Drug A group’s follow-up SBP showed a sample mean of \(\bar{x} = 128\) and sample standard deviation of \(s = 9\), based on \(n = 100\) patients. We want to test \(H_0: \mu = 130\) vs. \(H_A: \mu < 130\).
Recall the formula for a one-sample t-test statistic:
\[t_{obs} = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]

Fill in the code below to calculate the standard error and the test statistic, testing against \(\mu_0 = 130\).

# summary statistics
xbar = mean(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
mu0 = 130
s = sd(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
n = sum(htn_trial$group_num==1)

# print values
xbar ;  s; n

# standard error
se =  / sqrt()

# test statistic
t_obs = ( - ) / 
t_obs






Solution





# summary statistics
xbar = mean(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
mu0 = 130
s = sd(htn_trial$sbp_followup[htn_trial$group_num==1])
n = sum(htn_trial$group_num==1)

# print values
xbar ; s; n

# standard error
se = s / sqrt(n)

# test statistic
t_obs = (xbar - mu0) / se
t_obs
[[1] 127.3865 [1] 130 [1] 8.059693 [1] 100 [1] -3.24262{style=“font-family: ‘Monaco’; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;”}
Our observed test statistic is negative, consistent with a sample mean (127.4) that’s below the hypothesized value (130).






Since \(H_A: \mu < \mu_0\), this is a one-sided, lower-tailed test. The rejection region is in the left tail of the \(t\) distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom.

Find the critical value (rejection region cutoff) for a lower-tailed test with \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(n - 1 = 99\) degrees of freedom.

# significance level
alph = 

# lower-tailed rejection region cutoff
qt(alph, df = )






Solution





# significance level
alph = 0.05

# lower-tailed rejection region cutoff
qt(alph, df = n - 1)
[1] -1.660391
Since our observed test statistic (-3.24) is more negative than this cutoff (-1.66), it falls in the rejection region.




Based on the rejection region above, would we reject or fail to reject \(H_0\)? What would that mean in the context of this study?






Calculate the one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value corresponding to our test statistic, using pt(). Since we want the area to the left of our test statistic, we can use the default lower.tail = TRUE (the default, so you don’t need to specify it).

# one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value
pt(t_obs, df = )






Solution





# one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value
pt(t_obs, df = n - 1)
[1] 0.0008073392
This p-value (0.0008) is less than 0.05, so we would reject \(H_0\) and conclude that average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group is below 130—consistent with our rejection region result above.






A one-sided 95% confidence interval for \(H_A: \mu < \mu_0\) has the form \(\left(-\infty, \ \bar{x} + t^* \cdot se\right)\), where \(t^*\) is the upper 95th-percentile critical value (note: this is a different cutoff than the one we used for the rejection region above, since that one captured the lower 5% rather than the upper 5%).

Calculate the upper bound of a one-sided 95% confidence interval for the population mean follow-up SBP.

# one-sided 95% CI upper bound
xbar + qt(, df = ) * se






Solution





# one-sided 95% CI upper bound
xbar + qt(0.95, df = n - 1) * se
[1] 128.7248
We are 95% confident that the true average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group is no more than about 128.7—which is indeed below our threshold of 130. This agrees with our rejection region and p-value results, as it should, since all three methods lead to the same conclusion.






All of this can be done in a single step using the built-in t.test() function.

Fill in the code below to run a one-sample t-test on the Drug A group’s sbp_followup, testing against \(\mu_0 = 130\) with the alternative hypothesis that the mean is less than 130.

# one-sample t-test
drug_a_followup = htn_trial %>% filter( == 1) %>% pull(sbp_followup)
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = , alternative = )






Solution





# one-sample t-test
drug_a_followup = htn_trial %>% filter(group_num == 1) %>% pull(sbp_followup)
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "less")
We can see that the numbers here match out by-hand calculations.




Compare the output of t.test() to our manual calculations above. Are the general conclusions (reject vs. fail to reject) consistent?






Modify the code above to run the same test, but using a two-sided alternative instead.

# two-sided one-sample t-test
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = , alternative = )

title: Module 5: Categorical Data, Part III
text:
Fisher’s exact test is used for the same kind of question as the chi-squared test of independence/homogeneity (is there an association between two categorical variables?), but it doesn’t rely on the chi-squared approximation—which breaks down when expected cell counts are small. Instead, it calculates an exact p-value based on the hypergeometric distribution.
Rule of thumb: if any expected cell count in your table is below 5, prefer Fisher’s exact test over the chi-squared test.
Motivating example: In a small safety sub-study, researchers compared the rate of a rare severe allergic reaction between two vaccine brands. Out of 25 patients given Brand X, 1 had a severe reaction (24 did not). Out of 20 patients given Brand Y, 5 had a severe reaction (15 did not). Is there an association between vaccine brand and reaction rate?


Here’s our table of counts, with rows for vaccine brand and columns for reaction status:
# table of counts: rows = vaccine brand, columns = reaction (yes, no)
tbl = matrix(c(1, 24, 5, 15), nrow = 2, byrow = T)
rownames(tbl) = c("Brand X", "Brand Y")
colnames(tbl) = c("Reaction", "No Reaction")
tbl




Fill in the code below to check the expected cell counts using chisq.test()$expected (even though we won’t trust the chi-squared p-value itself, this is still a quick way to check the expected counts).

# expected counts under chi-squared assumptions
chisq.test(, correct = F)$expected






Solution





# expected counts under chi-squared assumptions
chisq.test(tbl, correct = F)$expected
Two of the four expected counts (around 3.3 and 2.7) are below 5—the chi-squared test’s assumptions are violated here. This is exactly the situation Fisher’s exact test is designed for.




Why does a small expected cell count cause problems for the chi-squared test specifically? (Hint: think about what the chi-squared distribution is approximating, and how well that approximation works with very few observations in a cell.)






Fill in the code below to run Fisher’s exact test on the table.

# Fisher's exact test
fisher.test()






Solution





# Fisher's exact test
fisher.test(tbl)
[1] p-value = 0.07409, odds ratio = 0.1253912
With a p-value of about 0.074, we’re just above the conventional 0.05 threshold—not quite enough evidence to conclude the reaction rates differ between brands, though the estimated odds ratio (about 0.13, meaning the odds of a reaction are much lower for Brand X) suggests this might be worth investigating with a larger sample.




Fisher’s exact test gave us a p-value, but we didn’t need to specify a test statistic or distribution (like we would for a t-test or chi-squared test) to get there. In your own words, what is Fisher’s exact test actually calculating to arrive at this p-value?






For comparison, fill in the code below to run the (technically invalid, given our small expected counts) chi-squared test on the same table, and compare the p-values.

# chi-squared test (for comparison only - not actually valid here!)
chisq.test(, correct = F)






Solution





# chi-squared test (for comparison only - not actually valid here!)
chisq.test(tbl, correct = F)
R may give a warning here (something like “Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect”) precisely because of the small expected counts we checked earlier. The resulting p-value may be noticeably different from Fisher’s exact p-value—a good illustration of why checking conditions matters before trusting a test’s output.




Even if R lets you run chisq.test() without an error (just a warning), why is it important not to just use whichever test gives you the smaller p-value?

title: Module 5: Categorical Data, Part II
text:
The chi-squared (\(\chi^2\)) test shows up in three related but distinct situations, all based on comparing observed counts to expected counts:

Goodness-of-fit: does a single categorical variable follow a specified distribution?
Homogeneity: does the distribution of a categorical variable differ across two or more groups?
Independence: are two categorical variables associated with each other?

All three use the same test statistic:
\[\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}\]
where \(O\) is an observed count and \(E\) is the count we’d expect under \(H_0\), summed over all cells of a table.

text:
Goodness-of-Fit
This version tests whether a single categorical variable follows a specified set of proportions.
Motivating example: At a flu clinic, lab testing identified which flu strain (A, B, or C) was responsible for each of 200 confirmed flu cases this season. Historically, strains are distributed as 50% A, 30% B, 20% C. This season, the observed counts were: 80 Strain A, 70 Strain B, 50 Strain C. Does this season’s distribution differ from the historical pattern?

Expected Counts

Fill in the code below to calculate the expected count for each strain, under the historical proportions (50%, 30%, 20%), out of 200 total cases.

# observed counts
obs = c(80, 70, 50)

# expected counts under historical proportions
exp_props = c(, , )
exp_counts = exp_props * 
exp_counts






Solution

# expected counts under historical proportions
exp_props = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
exp_counts = exp_props * 200
exp_counts
[1] 100 60 40
We’d expect 100 Strain A cases, 60 Strain B, and 40 Strain C under the historical distribution—but we observed 80, 70, and 50. There’s a noticeable shift toward Strains B and C this season.





Calculating the Test Statistic

Fill in the code below to calculate the chi-squared test statistic by hand.

# chi-squared test statistic
sum(( - exp_counts)^2 / )






Solution





# chi-squared test statistic
sum((obs - exp_counts)^2 / exp_counts)
[1] 8.166667
With \(k = 3\) categories, this statistic has \(k - 1 = 2\) degrees of freedom.





Using chisq.test()

# chi-squared goodness-of-fit test
chisq.test(, p = c(, , ), correct = F)

text:
Test of Homogeneity
This version compares the distribution of a categorical outcome across two or more independent groups—it’s really just a generalization of the two-proportion z-test (for a 2x2 table) to tables with more rows or columns.
Motivating example: Does flu infection rate differ between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients? Among 150 vaccinated patients, 9 got the flu (141 did not). Among 100 unvaccinated patients, 20 got the flu (80 did not).

Setting Up the Table
Here’s our table of counts, with rows for vaccination status and columns for flu status:
# table of counts: rows = vaccination status, columns = flu (yes, no)
tbl = matrix(c(9, 141, 20, 80), nrow = 2, byrow = T)
rownames(tbl) = c("Vaccinated", "Unvaccinated")
colnames(tbl) = c("Flu", "No Flu")
tbl


Checking Expected Counts
Before trusting the chi-squared approximation, let’s check that all the expected cell counts are large enough (the usual rule of thumb is at least 5).

Fill in the code below to extract the expected counts for this table. (You can pull these from chisq.test()’s output, even before looking at the p-value.)

# expected counts
chisq.test(, correct = F)$expected






Solution





# expected counts
chisq.test(tbl, correct = F)$expected
All four expected counts (about 17.4, 132.6, 11.6, and 88.4) are comfortably above 5, so the chi-squared approximation is valid here.





Running the Test

Fill in the code below to run the chi-squared test of homogeneity on this table.

# chi-squared test of homogeneity
chisq.test(, correct = F)






Solution





# chi-squared test of homogeneity
chisq.test(tbl, correct = F)

title: Module 3: Nonparametric Methods, Part I
text:
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the nonparametric alternative to the one-sample (or paired) t-test. Instead of assuming the data (or differences) are normally distributed, it only requires that the distribution be symmetric around its median. This makes it a useful option when sample sizes are small and the data look skewed, so we can’t confidently rely on the CLT.
Conditions:

Random sample
The distribution of differences is (approximately) symmetric around the median

\[H_0: \text{median} = m_0 \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad H_A: \text{median} \ne m_0 \ \ (\text{or} \ <, \ >)\]
Motivating example: Before launching the full hypertension trial, the research team ran a small pilot study with just 12 patients in the Drug A group, to get an early read on whether the drug had any effect at all. The changes in SBP (follow-up minus baseline) for these 12 patients are stored in pilot_change. With such a small sample, and visibly skewed values, we’re hesitant to assume normality—so we’ll use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test instead of a paired/one-sample t-test.

With only 11 of 12 values negative, and values ranging from -30 to +2, this small sample doesn’t look like a great candidate for assuming normality—a good case for a nonparametric test.






The signed-rank test works by: (1) taking the absolute difference from the hypothesized median (\(m_0 = 0\) here, since we’re testing whether SBP changed at all), (2) ranking those absolute differences from smallest to largest, and (3) summing the ranks of the positive differences (this sum is often called \(V\) or \(W^+\)).

A confidence interval for the average \(Y\) at a given \(X\) (how precisely do we know the mean?)
A prediction interval for an individual new observation at a given \(X\) (how much does any one person vary around that mean?)

Prediction intervals are always wider, since they account for both our uncertainty about the mean and the natural variability of individual observations.

title: Module 4: Comparing 3+ Groups
text:
ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) extends the two-sample t-test to three or more independent groups, testing whether any of the group means differ.
Conditions:

Random samples from each population
Independent samples (both within and across groups)
Equal variances across groups (a bigger concern here than in the two-sample case!)
Each group: \(n > 30\), or normally distributed in the population

\[H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad H_A: \text{at least one } \mu_i \text{ differs}\]
Motivating example: Suppose the hypertension trial was expanded to test a second drug (“Drug B”) alongside Drug A and Placebo—a 3-arm trial with 80 patients per arm. We want to know: does average SBP change differ across the three treatment groups?



Fill in the code below to create a factor column, group, from group_num (1 = Drug A, 2 = Drug B, 3 = Placebo).

# create a labeled factor variable
htn3 = htn3 %>%
  mutate(group = factor(, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                         labels = c(, , )))

head(htn3)






Solution





# create a labeled factor variable
htn3 = htn3 %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group_num, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                         labels = c("Drug A", "Drug B", "Placebo")))

head(htn3)
Now group has three labeled levels instead of the numeric codes.







Fill in the code below to create a boxplot of sbp_change by group, and calculate the sample size, mean, and sd within each group.

# boxplot
htn3 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = , y = , fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# summary statistics (saved for later use)
group_stats = htn3 %>%
  group_by() %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp_change), sd = sd())
group_stats






Solution





# boxplot
htn3 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = sbp_change, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# summary statistics (saved for later use)
group_stats = htn3 %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(sbp_change), sd = sd(sbp_change))
group_stats
You should see Drug A with the most negative (largest decrease) mean change, Drug B intermediate, and Placebo closest to 0. We’ve saved this as group_stats so we can reuse it below, rather than recalculating.






Let’s calculate the F-statistic directly from group_stats (the real sample sizes, means, and standard deviations we just computed from the data).
The ANOVA F-statistic compares the variance between groups to the variance within groups:
\[F = \dfrac{MSB}{MSW} = \dfrac{SSB / (k-1)}{SSW / (N-k)}\]
The code below walks through the calculation using the columns of group_stats—run it to see the grand mean, SSB, and SSW for our data.
# total sample size and number of groups
N = sum(group_stats$n)
k = 3

# grand mean (weighted average, here all n's equal so just the average)
grand_mean = sum(group_stats$n * group_stats$mean) / N
grand_mean

# sum of squares between groups
SSB = sum(group_stats$n * (group_stats$mean - grand_mean)^2)
SSB

# sum of squares within groups
SSW = sum((group_stats$n - 1) * group_stats$sd^2)
SSW
Since these are calculated directly from our simulated htn3 data, your exact numbers will be close to (but not identical to) a grand mean around -8.7, with Drug A pulling the grand mean down and Placebo pulling it up.

Now use SSB and SSW to calculate MSB, MSW, and the F-statistic.

# mean squares
MSB = SSB / ()
MSW = SSW / ()

# F statistic
F_obs = MSB / MSW
F_obs






Solution





# mean squares
MSB = SSB / (k - 1)
MSW = SSW / (N - k)

# F statistic
F_obs = MSB / MSW
F_obs
[1] 25.7227
Compared to a critical value of about 3.03 (from an F distribution with 2 and 237 degrees of freedom at \(\alpha = 0.05\)), you should find your observed F-statistic is far larger—strong evidence that at least one group mean differs from the others. (Share your exact number with me once you’ve run this, and I can update this solution text to match exactly, the same way we did for the two-sample t-test file!)






In R, we typically fit ANOVA as a linear model and then use anova() to get the F-test.

Fill in the code below to fit a linear model of sbp_change predicted by group, and print the ANOVA table.

# fit model and get ANOVA table
model = lm( ~ , data = htn3)
anova(model)






Solution





# fit model and get ANOVA table
model = lm(sbp_change ~ group, data = htn3)
anova(model)
Since our hand calculation above was computed directly from this same data (rather than from hypothetical summary statistics), the F-statistic and p-value here should match our hand-calculated F_obs almost exactly.






A significant ANOVA only tells us some group differs—it doesn’t say which. For that, we need pairwise comparisons, adjusted for the fact that we’re running multiple tests (to control the overall Type I error rate).

Fill in the code below to get all pairwise comparisons between groups, with a Bonferroni correction.

# pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction
model_emm = emmeans(model, pairwise ~ , adjust = )
model_emm$contrasts






Solution





# pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction
model_emm = emmeans(model, pairwise ~ group, adjust = "bonferroni")
model_emm$contrasts
Given how clearly separated the three group means are in group_stats, we’d expect all three pairwise comparisons to come out significant even after the Bonferroni correction: Drug A vs. Drug B, Drug A vs. Placebo, and Drug B vs. Placebo.




Why do we need to adjust for multiple comparisons when running all pairwise tests, instead of just using an unadjusted significance level of 0.05 for each one?





This is an important gotcha: if your grouping variable is stored as a number instead of a factor, R will (silently and incorrectly) treat it as a continuous predictor instead of a categorical one!

Fill in the code below to fit the incorrect model using the numeric group_num instead of the factor group, and compare its ANOVA table to the correct one.

# INCORRECT: treating group as numeric
model_incorrect = lm( ~ , data = htn3)
anova(model_incorrect)






Solution





# INCORRECT: treating group as numeric
model_incorrect = lm(sbp_change ~ group_num, data = htn3)
anova(model_incorrect)
This model now has only 1 degree of freedom for group_num instead of 2—because R is fitting a straight line through the numeric codes 1, 2, 3, rather than estimating a separate mean for each group. This is almost never what you want for a categorical predictor!




Why does it matter that group_num has only 1 degree of freedom in the incorrect model, while the properly-coded group factor has 2? What is R actually assuming about the relationship between the numeric codes and the outcome in the incorrect model?

Conditions:

title: Module 3: Nonparametric Methods, Part II
text:
The Wilcoxon rank-sum test (also called the Mann-Whitney U test) is the nonparametric alternative to the two-sample t-test. Instead of comparing means and requiring (approximate) normality, it compares the ranks of observations across two independent groups—testing whether one group tends to produce systematically larger (or smaller) values than the other.
Conditions:

Random samples from each population
Independent samples
(No normality assumption needed—this is the whole point of a nonparametric test!)

Motivating example: In a small pilot study, researchers recorded the number of days it took each patient’s blood pressure to reach a “controlled” level, comparing 10 patients on Drug A to 10 patients on Placebo. This “days to control” outcome is a count that’s likely to be right-skewed (most patients respond within a week or two, but a few take much longer)—a good candidate for a rank-based test rather than a t-test. The data are in pilot2, with columns days_to_control and group.

  ggplot(aes(x = , y = , color = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")






Solution





# boxplot of days to control, by group
pilot2 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = days_to_control, color = group)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
The Drug A group’s values should cluster noticeably lower than the Placebo group’s—Drug A patients seem to reach controlled blood pressure faster.






The rank-sum test works by combining both groups into one pool, ranking all observations together (smallest = rank 1), and then looking at whether one group’s ranks tend to be systematically higher or lower than the other’s.

  mutate(rank_all = rank())

  mutate(rank_all = rank(days_to_control))

pilot2
Notice some tied values get tied (averaged) ranks—for example, two patients with days_to_control = 4 would each get the average of the two ranks they’d otherwise occupy.







Fill in the code below to calculate the sum of the ranks within each group.

  group_by() %>%
  summarise(rank_sum = sum())






Solution

Drug A’s rank sum should be much lower than Placebo’s (around 56 vs. 155, out of a total of 210 across all 20 ranks)—exactly what we’d expect if Drug A patients tend to reach controlled blood pressure faster.




If the two groups had identical distributions (no real difference), roughly what would you expect the two rank sums to look like? How does that compare to what we found?

W = 0.5, p-value = 0.0001786
Because there are tied values in this data (e.g., two patients with days_to_control = 4), R can’t compute an exact p-value and will print a warning saying it’s using a normal approximation instead—that’s expected and fine here. text:
McNemar’s test is the categorical analog of the paired t-test: it’s used when a binary outcome is measured twice on the same subjects (e.g., before and after an intervention), rather than on two independent groups.
The key insight is that concordant pairs (subjects who gave the same answer both times) don’t tell us anything about change—only the discordant pairs (subjects whose status switched) matter. McNemar’s test asks: among the discordant pairs, is one direction of switching more common than the other?
\[H_0: \text{switching in each direction is equally likely} \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad H_A: \text{one direction is more common}\]
Motivating example: A clinic measured flu antibody protection status (Protected / Not Protected) in 120 patients, both before and after a booster shot. We want to know: did the booster shift patients toward being protected?
The results were:

After: Not Protected

Before: Not Protected

Notice the two diagonal cells (40 and 35) are the concordant pairs (status didn’t change), while the two off-diagonal cells (10 and 35) are the discordant pairs (status changed in one direction or the other).

\[\chi^2 = \dfrac{(b - c)^2}{b + c}\]
where \(b\) and \(c\) are the two discordant cell counts (here, \(b = 10\) patients went from Protected to Not Protected, and \(c = 35\) went from Not Protected to Protected).

A very small p-value—strong evidence that switching happened more often in one direction (Not Protected → Protected) than the other, consistent with the booster having a real effect.

This matches our hand calculation exactly.






McNemar’s test is actually equivalent to testing whether the proportion of discordant pairs going in one particular direction equals 0.5—i.e., a one-proportion test applied only to the discordant pairs!

Fill in the code below to run this as a one-proportion z-test: out of the 45 discordant pairs (\(b + c = 10 + 35 = 45\)), test whether the proportion that went from Not Protected to Protected (\(c = 35\)) differs from 0.5.

# one-proportion test on the discordant pairs
prop.test(x = , n = , p = , correct = F)






Solution





# one-proportion test on the discordant pairs
prop.test(x = 35, n = 45, p = 0.5, correct = F)
The test statistic here, when squared (\(z^2\)), should come out to the same value as our McNemar chi-squared statistic (13.889)—another example of the \(z^2 = \chi^2\) relationship we saw with the two-proportion z-test and chi-squared test of homogeneity.

Conditions:

Random sample from the population

Each of the 200 patients (100 per group) has a baseline systolic blood pressure (SBP, in mmHg) and a 12-week follow-up SBP. We’ll use this same trial throughout Module 3 to practice different tests. For this first test, we’ll focus on a simple question: is the average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group below the clinical hypertension threshold of 130 mmHg?

Since our observed test statistic (-2.22) is more negative than this cutoff (-1.66), it falls in the rejection region.




Based on the rejection region above, would we reject or fail to reject \(H_0\)? What would that mean in the context of this study?






Calculate the one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value corresponding to our test statistic, using pt(). Since we want the area to the left of our test statistic, we can use the default lower.tail = TRUE (the default, so you don’t need to specify it).

# one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value
pt(t_obs, df = )






Solution





# one-sided (lower-tailed) p-value
pt(t_obs, df = n - 1)
[1] 0.01427224
This p-value (0.014) is less than 0.05, so we would reject \(H_0\) and conclude that average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group is below 130—consistent with our rejection region result above.






A one-sided 95% confidence interval for \(H_A: \mu < \mu_0\) has the form \(\left(-\infty, \ \bar{x} + t^* \cdot se\right)\), where \(t^*\) is the upper 95th-percentile critical value (note: this is a different cutoff than the one we used for the rejection region above, since that one captured the lower 5% rather than the upper 5%).

Calculate the upper bound of a one-sided 95% confidence interval for the population mean follow-up SBP.

# one-sided 95% CI upper bound
xbar + qt(, df = ) * se






Solution





# one-sided 95% CI upper bound
xbar + qt(0.95, df = n - 1) * se
[1] 129.4944
We are 95% confident that the true average follow-up SBP in the Drug A group is no more than about 129.5—which is indeed below our threshold of 130. This agrees with our rejection region and p-value results, as it should, since all three methods lead to the same conclusion.






All of this can be done in a single step using the built-in t.test() function.

Fill in the code below to run a one-sample t-test on the Drug A group’s sbp_followup, testing against \(\mu_0 = 130\) with the alternative hypothesis that the mean is less than 130.

# one-sample t-test
drug_a_followup = htn_trial %>% filter( == 1) %>% pull(sbp_followup)
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = , alternative = )






Solution





# one-sample t-test
drug_a_followup = htn_trial %>% filter(group_num == 1) %>% pull(sbp_followup)
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "less")
Since htn_trial is simulated data, the exact numbers won’t match our hand calculation above exactly—but they should tell a similar story, given that we simulated this group’s follow-up SBP with a true mean around 128.




Compare the output of t.test() to our manual calculations above. Are the general conclusions (reject vs. fail to reject) consistent, even if the exact numbers differ slightly?






Modify the code above to run the same test, but using a two-sided alternative instead.

# two-sided one-sample t-test
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = , alternative = )






Solution





# two-sided one-sample t-test
t.test(drug_a_followup, mu = 130, alternative = "two.sided")
The test statistic stays the same, but the p-value roughly doubles compared to the one-sided test, and the confidence interval becomes two-sided (both a lower and upper bound) instead of having an infinite lower bound.




In general, when is it appropriate to use a one-sided test instead of a two-sided test? Why is it considered poor practice to choose the direction of a one-sided test after looking at your data?

title: Module 3: Inference for Numerical Outcomes, Part I
text:
Sample Size and Power
Before collecting data, we often want to know how large a sample we’ll need to detect a meaningful effect, or how much power a given sample size will provide. R’s power.t.test() function handles this for one-sample (and paired) t-tests.

Suppose we want to detect a true difference (delta) of 2 mmHg from the null value, assuming a standard deviation of 9, with a significance level of 0.05 and 80% power, using a one-sided test. Fill in the code below to find the required sample size.

# required sample size for 80% power
power.t.test(delta = , sd = , sig.level = ,
             power = , type = , alternative = )






Solution





# required sample size for 80% power
power.t.test(delta = 2, sd = 9, sig.level = 0.05,
             power = 0.8, type = "one.sample", alternative = "one.sided")
n = 126.5606
We would need about 127 participants (always round up!) to have an 80% chance of detecting a true difference of 2 mmHg, if one exists.




Now suppose we only have 100 participants available (as in our actual Drug A group). Fill in the code below to calculate the power of our test under the same assumptions (delta = 2, sd = 9, one-sample, one-sided).

# power with n = 
power.t.test(n = 100, delta = , sd = ,
             type = , alternative = )






Solution





# power with n = 100
power.t.test(n = 100, delta = 2, sd = 9,
             type = "one.sample", alternative = "one.sided")
power = 0.71299
With 100 participants, our power is about 71.3%—a bit short of the 80% we were aiming for.




Based on what you know about power, would you expect this power (71.3%) to be higher or lower if we used a two-sided test instead of one-sided? What about if the true effect size (delta) were larger, say 4 instead of 2? You can check your intuition by modifying the code above.

title: Module 5: Categorical Data, Part II
text:
Fisher’s Exact Test
Fisher’s exact test is used for the same kind of question as the chi-squared test of independence/homogeneity (is there an association between two categorical variables?), but it doesn’t rely on the chi-squared approximation—which breaks down when expected cell counts are small. Instead, it calculates an exact p-value based on the hypergeometric distribution.
Rule of thumb: if any expected cell count in your table is below 5, prefer Fisher’s exact test over the chi-squared test.
Motivating example: In a small safety sub-study, researchers compared the rate of a rare severe allergic reaction between two vaccine brands. Out of 25 patients given Brand X, 1 had a severe reaction (24 did not). Out of 20 patients given Brand Y, 5 had a severe reaction (15 did not). Is there an association between vaccine brand and reaction rate?

Setting Up the Table
Here’s our table of counts, with rows for vaccine brand and columns for reaction status:
# table of counts: rows = vaccine brand, columns = reaction (yes, no)
tbl = matrix(c(1, 24, 5, 15), nrow = 2, byrow = T)
rownames(tbl) = c("Brand X", "Brand Y")
colnames(tbl) = c("Reaction", "No Reaction")
tbl


Checking Expected Counts

Fill in the code below to check the expected cell counts using chisq.test()$expected (even though we won’t trust the chi-squared p-value itself, this is still a quick way to check the expected counts).

# expected counts under chi-squared assumptions
chisq.test(, correct = F)$expected






Solution





# expected counts under chi-squared assumptions
chisq.test(tbl, correct = F)$expected
Two of the four expected counts (around 3.3 and 2.7) are below 5—the chi-squared test’s assumptions are violated here. This is exactly the situation Fisher’s exact test is designed for.




Why does a small expected cell count cause problems for the chi-squared test specifically? (Hint: think about what the chi-squared distribution is approximating, and how well that approximation works with very few observations in a cell.)




Running Fisher’s Exact Test

Fill in the code below to run Fisher’s exact test on the table.

# Fisher's exact test
fisher.test()






Solution





# Fisher's exact test
fisher.test(tbl)
[1] p-value = 0.07409, odds ratio = 0.1253912
With a p-value of about 0.074, we’re just above the conventional 0.05 threshold—not quite enough evidence to conclude the reaction rates differ between brands, though the estimated odds ratio (about 0.13, meaning the odds of a reaction are much lower for Brand X) suggests this might be worth investigating with a larger sample.




Fisher’s exact test gave us a p-value, but we didn’t need to specify a test statistic or distribution (like we would for a t-test or chi-squared test) to get there. In your own words, what is Fisher’s exact test actually calculating to arrive at this p-value?




Comparing to the Chi-Squared Test

For comparison, fill in the code below to run the (technically invalid, given our small expected counts) chi-squared test on the same table, and compare the p-values.

# chi-squared test (for comparison only - not actually valid here!)
chisq.test(, correct = F)






Solution





# chi-squared test (for comparison only - not actually valid here!)
chisq.test(tbl, correct = F)
R may give a warning here (something like “Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect”) precisely because of the small expected counts we checked earlier. The resulting p-value may be noticeably different from Fisher’s exact p-value—a good illustration of why checking conditions matters before trusting a test’s output.




Even if R lets you run chisq.test() without an error (just a warning), why is it important not to just use whichever test gives you the smaller p-value?
